title: Testing the height-to-mass table
variables: h is numerical height in feet. M is the proposed mass in pounds. The source uses 3.28 feet per meter and 2.2 pounds per kilogram.
domain: Positive height in the units chosen by the author.
test: One meter computes to 35.29 pounds, two to 282.30 and four to 2,258.40. This checks the table’s arithmetic, not a claim about human physiology.
interpretation: Cubing the given height reproduces the later rows of the source table to its printed precision, but misses the first by a factor of approximately eight.
dimensions: To map a length cubed to mass requires a density and shape factor. Entering feet and reporting pounds implicitly fixes a coefficient of 1 lb/ft³ in this convention.
issue: At one meter the text prints 282.30 pounds. The stated conversion and formula give 35.287552 pounds. The printed value would fit two meters. Relabeling the row is conjectural.

title: Three inequivalent counts for fictional copies
variables: a and b are the originator’s and copy’s ratings on the subscripted class. n counts additional fictional copies.
domain: Positive baselines. Ordinary bodies are counted in whole numbers, but the expressions can give fractions.
test: The printed 43 versus 19 C1 example gives 250.19 before any integer convention. The three-branch example uses 20 and 10 to expose the inequivalence.
interpretation: #128 proposes a difference in C1, a square root of a C3 ratio, and a C2 ratio as successive readings. It acknowledges that a proposed restatement produces a different number. It also switches from DP to PL for temporary copies.
dimensions: Ratios of like scales have no dimensions. A fractional game count requires further interpretation.
issue: Giving the source and copy 20 and 10 C1 produces 9, about 7.56, and about 3.93 respectively after actual class conversion. Choosing a branch changes the fiction.

title: A factorial proposed for strength
variables: d is C1 DP. W is a number described as pounds.
domain: The ordinary factorial needs a nonnegative integer argument. The quotient needs d > 0 and d ≠ 1.
test: The equality 4! = 24 is correct. Substituting 4 C1 into the printed composite formula does not reproduce that example.
interpretation: Rule 78 combines a logarithmic quotient with a factorial, then illustrates four factorial. At a given d these are two distinct operations.
dimensions: Using factorial on a rating gives a number. Pounds enter by the fictional calibration.
issue: With d = 4 the inner quotient is about 6.644, not four and not an integer. A gamma extension or a rounding rule would be an editorial addition.

title: Speed from a ship’s engine and hull ratings
variables: B is the hull-size increment and E the engine rating, both in C2 PL. The text sets its two hull variables equal.
domain: B > 0 for a positive base and nonzero denominator.
test: With an editorial hull rating of 4 and engine rating of 12, the number is 2² = 4 mph.
interpretation: A ratio sets an exponent, and the square root of the hull rating sets its base. This yields a calculation with both ship measurements fixed.
dimensions: The result is assigned mph by convention. Treating physical size or engine output as raw inputs would require independent calibration.
issue: The author in #177 calls #132 a favorite. The alternatives in #155 and #178 use different inputs and transforms.

title: A speed from linked C1 and C2 values
variables: p₁ and p₂ are C1 and C2 PL, represented as corresponding ratings in the examples. v is the velocity numeral.
domain: Both class ratings must be positive.
test: 10 C1 and 10 C2 give about 200.72 mph. The numerical agreement with a printed approximation does not select this law over the other speed rules.
interpretation: A model using both natural and common logs is different from the body-subtraction model of #155. At equal class magnitude p₁ = p₂ = 10, the exponent reduces to ln 10.
dimensions: The result is assigned mph. There is no derivation of its unit from the rating scales.
issue: At 20 C1 and the unrounded equivalent C2, the exponent is about 5.07. The printed hundred-thousand estimate uses a rounded exponent.

title: The calendar as a version number
variables: Y is the calendar year, V the web-version label, P the stated percentage of completeness.
domain: Applies to the dated convention given in #0, including its stated extension to a year before 2000.
test: 2002 gives version 0.2 and the stated 20% completion. There is no component-level denominator behind it.
interpretation: The formula yields the labels in the opening example. It offers no counting procedure for all parts needed to complete a game.
dimensions: A calendar-year difference is converted into a label and then a percentage. Neither is a measure of actual development effort.
issue: The masthead’s declared proportion is an editorial fact about the source's self-description. Earlier versions also changed labels, limiting the use of this dating formula.

title: Rolling a starting magnitude
variables: d₁ is starting C1 DP. Each roll is a face on one of the selected dice.
domain: One or more ordinary dice of specified size. The case is introduced as a tentative d20 version.
test: Three sixes produce 18 C1 DP. A d20 can instead reach 20, with a very different probability of any given total.
interpretation: In the named examples the die total gives the numerical baseline, while the choice of dice sets a ceiling and a distribution.
dimensions: C1 DP points per pip on the chosen build route.
issue: Rolling an actual baseline is possible. The initial choice of a pool, available abilities and their costs still affect the rest of the character.

title: Building a low-powered mutant by successive choices
variables: dⱼ is C2 DP after the jth advantage. j is its positive index in this construction.
domain: Positive integer j in this specific build sequence.
test: From 9 C2 the illustrated stages reach 18, 27, 36 and optionally 45. The distinct abilities purchased must be read from this example.
interpretation: #123 lists a rule of thumb for successively increasing denominators and offers a choice of effects at each stage. The resulting product telescopes to (j + 1) times the starting rating.
dimensions: Dimensionless multipliers applied to a C2 baseline.
issue: This worked sequence is more specific than the general permission to repeat modifiers. No session-to-session award trigger is given.

title: Doubling before or after class conversion
variables: x is a C2 input in the worked case. f is the adjacent-class transform.
domain: Positive x.
test: Doubling 49.28 after class conversion gives roughly 98.56. First doubling 20 and then converting gives roughly 368.63.
interpretation: #46 uses separate placements of a factor of two in its notation. Their order materially changes the result.
dimensions: The outputs compare scaled C3 ratings under two conventions.
issue: Two expressions may both include the same multiplier and class names while producing different values.

title: A proposed Defense and Body calibration
variables: p₂ is a C2 PL rating in #183’s HERO comparison. DEF and BOD are proposed external statistics.
domain: Positive rating and an applicable external comparison.
test: If 40 C2 PL is supplied, this branch assigns 20 each to DEF and BOD.
interpretation: Rule 183 offers two half-rated attributes, also allowing an alternative interpretation of their sum in terms of strength.
dimensions: Game-point equivalents in a HERO comparison.
issue: The author gives no rule here that subtracts rolled damage, recovers points over time, or treats BOD as a universal HYBRID pool.

title: Time reach in the astral-form proposal
variables: d₁ is C1 DP. Y is the stated reach in years.
test: 20 C1 DP gives one year. At 40 C1 DP the result has already reached 10,000 years.
interpretation: An affine change of rating followed by a square and a power of ten interpolates a short list of travel ranges.
dimensions: Calibration in fictional years. Its numerical constants have no independent empirical derivation here.
issue: Its squared exponent resembles the foundational transform, but the input is shifted and scaled directly rather than replaced by its logarithm.

title: Fictional range at a supplied warp number
variables: d₁ is C1 DP and W the warp number. R is range.
domain: d₁ ≥ 0, positive W in the worked case.
test: At warp 10 and 90 C1 DP, the stated range is 59,049 light-years.
interpretation: One of several local travel calibrations expresses distance as a power of the rating. Both warp index and baseline must already be known.
dimensions: In light-years. This is distance and not speed unless a time interval is added.
issue: The source distinguishes maximum from optimal performance. It does not establish a general relation to #30’s speed choices.

title: Proportional rescaling
variables: h₁ and d₁ are a reference height and C3 rating, and h₂ and d₂ the corresponding desired pair.
domain: Nonzero reference d₁ and common units for paired inputs.
test: For an editorial reference height of 2 units at 30 C3, 45 C3 predicts 3 of the same units.
interpretation: Knowing a reference character and a new rating gives a predicted height under a constant-ratio assumption.
dimensions: The C3 ratio is dimensionless and the result carries the reference length unit.
issue: The equation does not supply a universal choice of reference, and other height equations can give different predictions.

title: Pricing a fictional cyborg
variables: S is a fictional creation cost in dollars and d₂ the resulting C2 DP.
test: At one million dollars the rating is 25 C2. At six million it is about 33.39.
interpretation: A construct’s quoted cost is transformed into a rating. The calibration fits a familiar science-fiction title.
dimensions: The logarithm takes the numeric price in dollars. A change of currency needs recalibration.
issue: The appearance of a squared logarithm here does not mean that the equation equals the adjacent-class transform.

title: Class rating consumed by a spaceship’s body
variables: p₂ is total C2 PL. B is COM in the ship-body or size sense, also expressed in C2 PL.
domain: The worked interpretation uses p₂ ≥ B.
test: For an editorial net rating of eight points the formula returns the speed numeral 100.
interpretation: Subtract body cost before converting the remaining capability to a speed. This is a concrete use of COM away from appearance.
dimensions: The text alternates kilometers and miles per hour without changing the numerical calculation.
issue: Rules 155 and 158 discuss fuel and propose other calibrations. A common ship rating alone does not assign a unique speed in physical units.

title: A fictional bureaucracy by square root
variables: N is the population of the cyborg collectivity, p = log₁₀ N, and B the bureaucratic subpopulation.
domain: N > 0 when represented by its logarithm.
test: One million drones implies a bureaucracy of one thousand under this fictional rule.
interpretation: The two displayed forms are genuinely equivalent. A square root of an existing population is mathematical scaling quite apart from class conversion.
dimensions: The output is a number of fictional beings. A non-square N requires a rounding policy for a discrete count.
issue: The author supplies a square population example and no evidence for applying the law to real societies.

title: One step along the class scale
variables: x is the numerical value on one class scale. y is the equivalent value on the next.
domain: Real arithmetic requires x > 0. Rule examples generally use x ≥ 1.
test: 20 C2 → 49.28095 C3. The value 20 C1 → 49.28095 C2 uses the same arithmetic on a different pair of classes.
interpretation: Carries LS, PL or DP from CA to C1, C1 to C2, or C2 to C3. The same calculation appears for C3 to C4. It supplies a magnitude once an input exists.
dimensions: Dimensionless point ratings on specified classes. Taking a logarithm of a physical length would require a reference unit.
issue: The preface associates the expression with allocation. It supplies neither a starting budget nor a price list. C0 is handled separately.

title: Reading a scale backwards
variables: y is a value on the destination scale. x is a possible original rating.
domain: y ≥ 1. At y = 1 both branches give 1. No real solution for 0 < y < 1.
test: 35 C3 yields about 17.483 C2 on the increasing branch. For y = 10 the two possible inputs are 10 and 0.1.
interpretation: Writing x as 10ᵘ turns the forward transform into 10^(u²). Taking logs loses the sign of u. Rule 188 calls for a backwards conversion. Its example uses a rating above one.
dimensions: Dimensionless numerical class coordinates.
issue: The plus branch recovers x ≥ 1. Treating this as the sole inverse everywhere discards the reciprocal solution.

title: Repeated changes of class
variables: n counts class steps. u = log₁₀ x.
domain: x > 0, n a nonnegative integer.
test: At 100 CA the successive exponents of ten are 2, 4, 16, 256 and 65,536 through C4. Working on logarithms avoids overflow.
interpretation: Each step squares the exponent of ten. This is a derivation of the repeated conversion, and explains the extraordinary values in #200.
dimensions: Dimensionless class ratings.
issue: Here fⁿ means applying f repeatedly. It does not mean taking a power of f(x). The values 1 and 10 are fixed on the positive real domain.

title: Exchanging lifespan and power
notation: (s + a, p − a) or (s / k, kp)
variables: s and p are current LS and PL on one scale. a is an offset and k a multiplier.
domain: Multiplicative trade requires k ≠ 0. Positive ratings and k > 0 suit the examples.
test: Starting at LS = PL = 40 C2, #183 chooses halving LS and doubling PL. Addition would produce a different power rating.
interpretation: The additive pair preserves the sum. The multiplicative pair preserves the product. Rule 3 also pairs a square root with squaring and a natural logarithm with its inverse.
dimensions: s and p must be comparable game ratings. The author keeps DP as a baseline.
issue: Decreasing LS from 40 to 20 under the two displayed operations gives PL 60 or 80. No single trade rate follows from the instruction to use opposite operations.

title: Converting lifespan to years
notation: Y = f(s)·m, with m = 22 − s below 20, otherwise 2
variables: s is C2 LS. f(s) is C3 LS. m is the multiplier and Y is lifespan in years.
domain: Written branches meet at s = 20. Uses positive s when the class conversion is applied.
test: 19 C2 LS gives about 129.52 years. At 20 the result falls to about 98.56 years.
interpretation: Rule 6 gives the C3 multiplier and a C2 boundary. Reading the alternative statement for m as the below-20 branch matches its example at 19 and preserves its explicit above-20 instruction.
dimensions: Years per C3 point is a fictional calibration.
issue: The formula for m appears unqualified immediately after the threshold. On this reading a higher s can reduce Y below 20. This is total lifespan, with no rule here for ageing one round.

title: From baseline to average attribute
variables: d is C2 DP. A is average Mind, Body and Soul.
domain: d ≥ 0 for the square root.
test: 16 C2 DP gives 4 AMBS. Doubling AMBS requires multiplying the C2 input by four.
interpretation: A supplies an aggregate character rating. Squaring A reverses the calculation.
dimensions: A is in AMBS units. It is distinct from the C2 rating.
issue: An average leaves multiple individual Mind, Body and Soul assignments possible.

title: A HERO point-total estimate
variables: d₁ is C1 DP and T₁ a proposed HERO total character point rating.
domain: Numerical game ratings.
test: A character at 100 C1 DP is assigned 1,000 points by this estimate.
interpretation: One reading of IQ also uses ten times C1 with PL at default. Rule 122 spells out DP as the input for the point translation.
dimensions: The factor of ten maps one game’s rating into another game’s points.
issue: Using an analogous score for intelligence and points is a design choice. These examples do not validate an intelligence measure.

title: An alternative HERO point total
variables: d₃ is C3 DP. T₂ is the alternative total.
domain: d₃ > 0.
test: 100 C1 → 10,000 C2 → 10¹⁶ C3. This method gives 1,600 points against 1,000 from the linear estimate.
interpretation: Rule 122 treats the difference between this estimate and the linear estimate as uncertainty. At large magnitudes the disagreement can be hundreds of points.
dimensions: Numerical point scales. A difference between formulas supplies no statistical error interval.
issue: Both totals concern the same character. Rule 122 leaves the reader with a range rather than a method for choosing a purchase budget.

title: Contextual conversions to C0 Psyche
variables: P₀ is C0 Psyche. The subscript on each d indicates the class carrying DP.
domain: The logarithmic quotient requires d₁ > 0 and d₁ ≠ 1.
test: 100 C1 gives 50 under the logarithmic quotient, and 100 if directly carried across.
interpretation: Rule 5 associates different character examples with each map. C0 can name the scale chosen for an external statistic or for a particular kind of being.
dimensions: All four outputs are called C0 Psyche. Their input classes differ.
issue: The alternatives form a set of proposals, not interchangeable identities. No selector for arbitrary new characters is supplied here.

title: A low-level superhuman strength rating
variables: d is C2 DP. q is C0 strength for the specified fictional character type.
domain: d ≥ 0 and q ≥ 0.
test: 40 C2 DP maps to 80 C0 strength and the inverse returns 40.
interpretation: The inverse follows by squaring the equation and taking a cube root. This is a local relation with a genuine algebraic inverse.
dimensions: Game rating to game rating. Conversion to pounds is a separate and disputed operation.
issue: The source changes the relationship for more powerful characters. The local success does not make it a universal map to C0.

title: Martial Arts Grade as a success fraction
variables: d is C2 DP. m is the combat success value termed MAG.
domain: d > 0. For d ≥ 1 the output is in [0,1). At smaller positive d it is negative.
test: 16 C2 DP gives 0.75, or 75% on the fractional interpretation.
interpretation: The source describes a percentage, although the expression returns a fraction. Expressing the output as a percentage requires multiplying by 100.
dimensions: Dimensionless fraction.
issue: A grade by itself does not assign an opponent, combine grades, or choose a die rule.

title: Optional pool of six-sided dice
variables: r is the numerical rating on the selected class, and n the number of six-sided dice.
domain: Requires integral n to use ordinary dice as written.
test: 18 C1 uses 3d6. A 24 C2 rating uses 4d6.
interpretation: Fixing a magnitude fixes the example pool. Two ratings of 18 on different classes both yield three dice despite representing different fictional power.
dimensions: Numerical class points per die. A six-sided die is a discrete object.
issue: No rounding method for a fractional number of dice is given in #17. Its examples establish the pool, not a single success convention.

title: A high-roll condition at a chosen class
variables: M is the pool maximum on the reading that the stated percentage applies to that maximum. roll is a total.
domain: Die totals are integers. Rule 35 uses 66%, while the preface describes two thirds.
test: 3d6 must total at least 12 on this reading. Fair dice yield 81 successful outcomes out of 216, a success probability of 37.5%.
interpretation: The examples supply the dice and a high threshold. Interpreting percent as a share of the maximum lets a reader run one test.
dimensions: Fraction of a possible dice total is not the probability of passing the test.
issue: The denominator is hypothetical. On a 25d6 stress test, 66% of 150 is 99 and two thirds is 100. Both yield 12 on 3d6. #188 instead uses low rolls in its examples.

title: A roll-under target from a proposed rating
notation: t = round(d₂ − b), with b = 10 in the worked case
variables: d₂ is the desired C2 rating for the source’s C3 example. The starting baseline b is ten in this example and can vary. t is an inclusive upper bound on the roll.
domain: The final example rounds to an integer after subtracting the local 10-point baseline.
test: The printed worked threshold and the recomputed threshold differ by one whole die point.
interpretation: A desire for a rating becomes a roll-under target. Other examples in the same rule work directly from desired bonuses. The roll procedure is partly adapted from other games.
dimensions: Threshold in die-total units. The rule’s target and a probability are different quantities.
issue: The printed 35 C3 → 17.7 C2 → 8 or less conflicts with the #45 inverse: about 17.483 gives 7 or less under the same rounding.

title: Trading a creator’s scale for permanence
variables: r is the retained numeral, while its class label changes.
domain: A specific fictional effect and creator are assumed.
test: 75 C2 becomes 75 C3 on this instruction. Equating magnitudes instead would yield a much larger C3 numeral.
interpretation: To make an effect permanent, the example demotes the creator’s own magnitude while retaining the written numeral. The former power status may return when the effect expires naturally.
dimensions: Changing the label with a fixed numeral usually changes the represented magnitude.
issue: Distinct from representing one unchanged magnitude in two classes. Trigger, duration and broader eligibility remain unclear.

title: Letter-coded power ratings
variables: i is a letter’s 1-based alphabet position. k is a multiplier selected under the letter rule.
domain: i from 1 through 26. Competing branch conditions need precedence.
test: X, the 24th letter, gives 120 in #55. Q is 170 under #58’s ten-times rule.
interpretation: #55 gives multipliers 5, 10 or 20 from tests on i + 1. #58 uses a direct ten times position for particular entity ratings.
dimensions: Letter labels are shorthand for numbers, which still need a C scale.
issue: For i = 5 the increment is both even and divisible by three. The examples do not state a precedence rule for all letters.

title: Two readings of an immortality rating
variables: i is C0 immortality, d₂ is C2 at default lifespan, and d₁ is C1 DP.
domain: Nonnegative game ratings. Source offers a class of beings as a qualification for the second form.
test: At 100 C2 the first expression gives 500 C0 immortality.
interpretation: Rule 31 explicitly acknowledges the discrepancy and distinguishes demi-gods from lesser figures in assessing the second relation.
dimensions: A C0 score is distinct from a lifespan in years.
issue: Testing 20 C1 at its equivalent 49.28 C2 gives about 246.40 by the first and 40 by the second. Choosing a context matters.

title: Fictional duplicate count
variables: dₐ and dᵦ are the creator’s and duplicate’s C3 DP. n is the count of additional fictional bodies.
domain: dᵦ > 0. Ordinary counts require a nonnegative integer result.
test: 100 C3 divided between a 50-point original and a 50-point duplicate gives one new body.
interpretation: Equal division into an original and one duplicate corresponds to a two-to-one ratio. The source calls this a fuzzy-logic case.
dimensions: Ratio of two ratings on the same scale.
issue: A general policy for fractional bodies or a weaker creator is absent. This fictional ontology has no biological interpretation.

title: A difference-based comparison
variables: dₕ and dₗ are higher and lower C2 DP. X is the modifier, set to 1 in the rule’s first case.
domain: dₕ ≥ dₗ in the written ordering.
test: For a nine-point difference and X = 1 the comparison yields 100. A nine-point difference does not have this interpretation outside the chosen model.
interpretation: The resulting quantity is presented as the number of lesser souls within a greater one. The source also compares this rule with its fictional-duplicate formula.
dimensions: Dimensionless game ratings calibrated as a count or relative magnitude.
issue: For identical ratings and X = 1 this gives 0.1. The answer is neither an identity ratio nor an integer count. No rule here translates it into a contest winner.

title: Speed on the logarithmic movement rule
variables: d is C2 DP or PL for #39. v is numerical speed in miles per hour. #63 uses a technology rating for sublight flight.
domain: v > 0. The inverse works for any real d.
test: A speed of 1,000 mph corresponds to 40 C2. At 20 C2 the inverse gives 10 mph.
interpretation: With the character’s rating given, this yields a running speed. It has a linear rule in log speed, without the squared logarithm of the class transform.
dimensions: The logarithm uses the numeral in mph, equivalent to dividing the speed by 1 mph.
issue: #64 supplies a different rule for a mutant’s movement. No timed race or test against an obstacle is specified.

title: Direct movement rating
variables: d₃ is a mutant or meta-human’s C3 rating. v is the numerical speed.
domain: Positive game rating.
test: A mutant given 20 C2 DP has 49.28 C3 DP. #64 then gives 49.28 mph versus 10 mph under #39.
interpretation: The numeral for speed simply repeats the numeral for the C3 rating. The rule gives a very high-powered example.
dimensions: One mph per C3 point is a declared fictional calibration.
issue: At overlapping ratings it conflicts with the running formula if the character’s movement is running. A mode-specific reconciliation would require an extra assumption.

title: Phasing or cloaking percentage
variables: r is total rating, b the base (usually 10 C2), and H the percentage of phasing or cloaking.
domain: b > 0. For X > (√801 − 1)/2, H exceeds 100.
test: 100 C2 with base 10 gives 55%. 150 on the same base gives 120%.
interpretation: A triangular-number expression measures the extent of a fictional power. #68 refers the reader back to this rule for invisibility.
dimensions: The output is in percentage points, not a probability in [0,1].
issue: The text does not supply a cap, an obstacle difficulty, or a test converting percent phasing into success against a particular wall.

title: Ghost reading and ghost percentage
variables: d is C2 DP on the normal campaign scale, k is the PK reading, and G a ghost percentage.
domain: Nonnegative game ratings. Another campaign base can use C1.
test: 50 C2 DP → 5 PK → 25% ghost.
interpretation: Two distinct rules link a ghost’s baseline to a meter-like reading and that reading to a percentage.
dimensions: The squared reading yields percentage points on the author’s scale.
issue: At readings above ten it exceeds 100. The text gives no general interpretation for that result.

title: A fictional teleport distance
variables: d₂ is identified first as C2 DP and later as PL. j distinguishes types of effect.
domain: d₂ ≥ 0 and j = 1, 2 or 3 in the listed cases.
test: On the spatial branch, a rating of 16 gives a range of 10 meters.
interpretation: #23 uses j = 2 for a spatial teleport and changes j for other kinds of movement. This normalization closes the printed unmatched parenthesis at the end of the exponent.
dimensions: The ordinary result uses meters. An exceptional narrative regime changes the unit to light-years.
issue: Changing the unit while retaining the numeric result changes the range. No general difficulty check or arrival rule accompanies it.

title: Two faster-than-light speed laws
variables: z is a warp number, with z = C2/Y. Y depends in part on ship length. c denotes light speed here.
domain: Finite z, in the source’s fictional faster-than-light context.
test: A warp number of 2 produces three or two times the speed of light.
interpretation: Two alternatives for the same warp number produce different speeds. Choosing either is enough to evaluate a single example.
dimensions: A multiple of light speed. No empirical claim follows from consistent arithmetic.
issue: At z = 2 the branches already disagree. Ship-size calibrations elsewhere also vary.

title: Mental-power promotion by relabeling
variables: r is the original rating. r′ is a numerical rating on a more powerful scale.
domain: Positive fictional ratings. #62 supplies a C3-to-C2 example.
test: A 10 C3 telekinetic stunt is assigned 20 C2 for its telepathic analogue.
interpretation: The very same numeric addition appears in a time-travel proposal and in pricing telepathy relative to telekinesis. A move one magnitude higher is illustrated by a smaller class index.
dimensions: Adding ten and then relabeling changes potency, unlike calculating the next class representation of the same potency.
issue: #62 gives a relative price for a matching stunt. It does not define a catalogue of base stunt costs.

title: Game damage dice from baseline
variables: d is a mutant’s C2 DP. n is a count of six-sided game damage dice.
domain: The supplied examples yield integer n. Other positive ratings can give fractions.
test: 30 C2 DP gives 9d6 under #146.
interpretation: #146 reuses a cross-system mapping of C2 DP to Mutants & Masterminds PL and reads the result as a pool of damage dice.
dimensions: Dice are game quantities. This relation has no interpretation as physical injury.
issue: #73 and #118 supply other pool conventions. Rolling the dice gives a number whose effect on a continuing character needs further rules.

title: One-use game damage pool
variables: p₃ is the C3 PL of the effect. n is a count of six-sided game dice.
domain: p₃ ≥ 1 for nonnegative n. Fractional n has no defined die convention here.
test: 49 C3 PL gives 6d6 with the subtraction, 7d6 without it.
interpretation: The square-root version is identified with a one-use maximum. #118 also names a variant without the subtraction.
dimensions: Dice are a game score. This is not a conversion from a game result to real harm.
issue: Neither branch explains how to resolve fractional pools, subtract a defense, or update a character’s state.

title: Ideal proportions of character aspects
variables: K is karma (mental attributes), P powers, H health (physical attributes).
domain: Three proportional entries. The source does not prescribe a total.
test: For an illustrative supplied total of 24, the corresponding allocation is 4, 8 and 12.
interpretation: The ratio is presented as desirable for an ideal character or object. Normalizing to a supplied finite total is an editorial calculation.
dimensions: Relative shares of a common numerical total if the normalization is chosen.
issue: The ratio neither grants a pool nor states that health is expended by hits. It cannot stand in for a damage track.

title: A minimum advantage increment
variables: c is a COM amount expressed on the C2 DP scale. d is the current baseline. a is the advantage fraction.
test: At c = d = 90 the minimum advantage is 1/9 and the new baseline is 100.
interpretation: The rule calculates a minimum modifier, then raises the baseline. Other figures receive special or stacked modifiers to match their powers.
dimensions: The modifier is dimensionless. Input COM in this example is already expressed in C2 points.
issue: The example’s chosen larger modifier need not equal the computed minimum. #147 permits repetition but gives no universal acquisition schedule.

title: Writing-time comparison
variables: T₁ is a reference work’s writing time. d₁ and d₂ are the reference and candidate writers’ C3 DP.
domain: d₂ > 0. The proposed shortcut assumes comparable projects.
test: Five years for a 50-point writer scales to 25 years for a 10-point writer doing comparable work.
interpretation: The time estimate is conditional on equivalent scope and depth. #96 explicitly presents more than one possible comparison model.
dimensions: A dimensionless rating ratio scales years to years.
issue: An outcome can be computed even though the source acknowledges disagreement with its soul model. This is not a tested model of writing.

title: A fictional waiting time after death
variables: d₃ is the relevant C3 rating. Y is the wait for a new fictional body.
domain: Nonnegative d₃, with limited applicability specified in #87.
test: If a 5-point C3 rating is granted in a covered case, the wait is 25 years.
interpretation: A rule can attach an interval to an already declared death. It supplies no procedure for declaring an ordinary character dead in the first place.
dimensions: Years per squared game-rating unit.
issue: The source varies the treatment by type of being and status in fictional dimensions. Continuing the same character sheet is unspecified.

title: Fictional grade from course load
variables: p₃ is C3 PL, L is a specified credit load, and g is grade average.
domain: L > 0. A term and a year are alternative load periods in the text.
test: 24 C3 PL over eight credits gives a 3.0 average. This alone supplies no advancement award for the character.
interpretation: A calibrated rating is divided by course load. #164 also gives a C2-based grade for a particular student category.
dimensions: C3 points per course-credit unit are assigned the units of a grade average.
issue: Ordinary maximum grades are not enforced by the expression. #89 sometimes calls the input DP after identifying it as PL.

title: Later annual income proposal
variables: d is C2 DP, S is a fictional annual dollar salary.
domain: #202 expressly excludes d ≤ 10 for this reading.
test: In #202, 30 C2 DP gives one million per year and 40 gives one billion.
interpretation: Rule 202 provides a later annual-income mapping. Rule 184’s mapping instead varies the period of payment with narrative circumstances.
dimensions: The output is numerically in dollars per year. Reusing the number in a different payment period changes the amount.
issue: No empirical basis is given for inferring real incomes or chance of employment from the game statistic.

title: Competing measures of technology
variables: TL is technology level here. p₁ and p₂ are C1 and C2 PL.
domain: Nonnegative game values. #145 describes a low technology range for its first alternative.
test: Putting 36 C2 through the second #145 relation returns TL 3, although the first uses TL 6.
interpretation: #8 gives a linear C1 relation. #145 presents two other equations and acknowledges their conflict. Solving the last gives p₂ = 4TL².
dimensions: All are game scales, not measurements of technological progress.
issue: At TL = 6 the first #145 relation would give 36 C2, while the inverse of the second gives 144. The text’s suggested exception fails its own equations.

title: Alternative ratings for appearance
variables: c is COM for the context selected by #197. d is on the indicated class scale.
domain: Positive numerical ratings.
test: At 20 C2, about 49.28 C3, the two estimates are about 11.90 and 9.
interpretation: The later proposal explicitly compares its result with an earlier mapping. Both assign a fictional appearance rating, with other branches elsewhere.
dimensions: Dimensionless game ratings. The source’s proposed links to social categories have no empirical foundation here.
issue: Different rules impose discriminatory classifications. These can be indexed and examined without presenting them as character requirements.

title: A diameter-based rating for fictional worlds
variables: D is a diameter stated as a numerical distance. d₂ is C2 DP.
domain: D > 0. A common specified length unit is necessary.
test: Entering a diameter numeral of 10,000 yields 636 C2 DP.
interpretation: A logarithmic mapping allows a reader to assign or invert a celestial game rating.
dimensions: The source permits a numeral in miles or kilometers. A fixed physical diameter has different numerals in those units, hence different ratings.
issue: The factor 159 is a stated calibration. Nothing in the class transform derives that factor or establishes an astronomical law.

title: A label that looks like an infinite power
variables: X is the position of a letter. The infinity symbol is used as an assigned label.
domain: For ordinary exponentiation with X + 1 > 1, the limit as the exponent grows is unbounded.
test: The assigned figure is 100 at CA. In ordinary arithmetic, already 2¹⁰ is 1,024 and powers continue growing.
interpretation: The source fits an assigned value to a fictional figure. Its following sequence of class exponents is independently calculable from #45.
dimensions: A symbolic nickname and a real-valued limit have different mathematical types.
issue: For X = 1, a base of two does not tend to 100 as its exponent increases. No mathematical correction is offered; the finite game assignment is recorded separately.
